draft.title: Fuel cells
card: A fuel cell is a galvanic cell that is fed reactants from outside, so it keeps running as long as the supply lasts. A fuel such as hydrogen goes to one electrode and oxygen goes to the other.
In an acidic hydrogen fuel cell, hydrogen is oxidised at the anode: H2(g) → 2H+(aq) + 2e-. Oxygen is reduced at the cathode: O2(g) + 4H+(aq) + 4e- → 2H2O(l).
The electrons travel through the external circuit and make the electric current. The overall reaction is 2H2(g) + O2(g) → 2H2O(l), so the only product is water.
A battery has a fixed amount of reactants inside it and goes flat when they run out. A fuel cell does not go flat while fuel and oxygen keep being supplied.
draft.remember: A fuel cell makes electricity from a continuous supply of fuel and oxygen. A hydrogen fuel cell makes only water.

a.q: Which feature makes a fuel cell different from a standard battery?
opts: Its reactants are supplied continuously from outside
Its electrodes are not involved in any redox reaction
Its reaction runs without any electrons being transferred
Its anode is where reduction takes place
a.why: A fuel cell is fed fuel and oxygen from outside, so it can keep producing electricity. It still relies on redox reactions, with oxidation at the anode, so the other options are wrong.
a.clue: Think about what happens when a battery's reactants run out.

b.q: Mia's hydrogen fuel cell runs an acidic cell for a long trip. Hydrogen and oxygen are fed in the whole time. Which statement about the cell is correct?
opts: Hydrogen is oxidised at the anode and water is the product
Hydrogen is reduced at the cathode and water is the product
Oxygen is oxidised at the anode and hydrogen is the product
Hydrogen is oxidised at the anode and the cell soon goes flat
b.why: Hydrogen loses electrons, so it is oxidised at the anode, and oxygen is reduced to water at the cathode. The last option is tempting because it has the right electrode, but a fuel cell keeps running while it is fed.
b.clue: Which reactant loses electrons, and what does the supply do to the cell?

The distractor 'Its electrodes are not involved in any redox reaction' is slightly ambiguous. Fuel cell electrodes are usually inert and not consumed, unlike many battery electrodes, so a student could read 'involved' as 'reacting'. Redox does happen at the electrodes, so the option is still wrong, but clearer wording would help, for example 'No redox reaction takes place at its electrodes.'
